Baby & Child

Tetralogy of Fallot: diagnosis, treatment and lifelong care

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Tetralogy of Fallot, or TOF, is a combination of four heart changes present from birth. They can limit blood flow to the lungs and allow oxygen-poor blood to reach the body. Some babies become blue or grey, while others have little visible colour change at first. The exact anatomy and oxygen levels guide treatment. Surgery can improve circulation, but regular congenital-heart care remains important throughout life.

The narrowed lung pathway and the hole in the heart

One change is narrowing of the route from the right ventricle, the lower right pumping chamber, to the lungs. It can involve muscle below the pulmonary valve, the valve itself or the pulmonary arteries. In a severe form the valve opening is absent or closed, called pulmonary atresia. This is more than an isolated valve problem.

Another change is a ventricular septal defect, or VSD: a hole in the wall between the two lower chambers. Its effect depends on the pressure and resistance in the lung pathway. With substantial obstruction, oxygen-poor blood can cross toward the body’s circulation rather than reaching the lungs to pick up oxygen. Not every person has the same degree of mixing or low oxygen.

The overriding aorta and thickened right ventricle

The aorta, the main artery carrying blood to the body, sits over the VSD instead of connecting only to the left ventricle. This is called an overriding aorta and allows it to receive blood from both ventricles. Together with the obstructed lung pathway, this can reduce the oxygen in blood reaching the body.

The right ventricle’s muscle becomes thicker because it pumps against increased resistance and pressure. This is right ventricular hypertrophy; it is not simply a response to the body wanting more oxygen. Some people also have other features, such as an atrial septal defect, a right-sided aortic arch or differences in the coronary arteries. The cardiology team maps the individual anatomy.

Symptoms and blue spells are variable

Possible signs include rapid or difficult breathing during feeding or activity, tiring easily, poor weight gain, irritability, prolonged crying and a heart murmur. Low oxygen may cause blue or grey lips, tongue or skin, fainting or seizures. Symptoms depend on blood flow; no blue colour at birth does not rule out TOF, and colour alone cannot diagnose it.

Some babies have a sudden drop in oxygen during crying, feeding or other stress. These episodes, called tet spells or hypercyanotic spells, may cause darker blue or grey colour, fast deep breathing, unusual distress and then floppiness or reduced responsiveness. They are not confined to one age window. Dehydration or illness can make a known condition less stable.

A blue or unresponsive baby needs emergency help

Call emergency services now for sudden blue or grey lips, tongue or face, breathing difficulty, a seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, marked floppiness or severe difficulty waking. These signs can have several causes and do not prove TOF. Do not delay help while trying to diagnose the colour change or waiting for a heart appointment.

For a child with diagnosed TOF, follow the cardiology team’s written spell plan while emergency help is being arranged. The team may have taught a knees-to-chest position and calming measures for that child; these are not a substitute for an ambulance or a general home treatment for an undiagnosed blue baby. Report a first spell or increasing spells promptly, even if the child improves, and follow the team’s instructions about urgent assessment.

How it is diagnosed before and after birth

A routine pregnancy ultrasound may raise suspicion, and a fetal echocardiogram gives a detailed view of the heart. Some cases are missed before birth; a reassuring routine scan cannot exclude every heart problem. Prenatal diagnosis allows the fetal and cardiac teams to plan delivery location and care after birth according to the baby’s needs.

After birth, a murmur, feeding difficulty, colour change or low oxygen can lead to echocardiography. A newborn pulse-oximetry screen can help detect TOF, but a passed screen does not rule out every critical heart defect. Diagnosis is usually made in infancy, although some less obvious cases are identified later. Further tests are selected to clarify anatomy and function, rather than every child needing every test.

Causes, genetics and risk without blame

TOF develops while the heart forms during pregnancy, and the cause is unknown in many cases. Some children have an associated genetic condition, such as 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, also called DiGeorge syndrome, or trisomy 21/Down syndrome. These are possibilities, not conditions present in everyone with TOF. Ask about appropriate genetic testing and counselling, particularly with other findings or a family history.

Research on congenital heart defects links some risks with pre-existing diabetes, certain medicines, smoking or infections such as rubella. Age, nutrition or alcohol exposure cannot establish the cause of an individual child’s TOF, and there is no universal age-40 boundary that diagnoses it. Review health, medicines and vaccinations before pregnancy, avoid alcohol during pregnancy and seek prompt maternity advice after rubella exposure. Do not stop prescriptions yourself or assume a parent is to blame.

Treatment may involve one operation or stages

TOF usually needs surgical repair. A complete repair closes the VSD with a patch and relieves the blocked route to the lungs; the exact valve and artery work depends on the anatomy. Treatment is commonly planned early in life, but timing is individual. Severe low oxygen or a spell can need urgent hospital treatment rather than waiting for a routine surgery date.

Some babies need an initial procedure to improve lung blood flow before full repair, such as a shunt or selected stent procedure. More complex anatomy may need a conduit between the right ventricle and pulmonary artery. The team explains the proposed approach, risks and recovery; no single operation or guaranteed result applies to every baby. Home positioning, supplements or medicines taken without specialist advice cannot repair the structural changes.

Follow-up continues after repair

Many people do well after treatment, but repair is not the end of care. Pulmonary-valve leakage, recurrent narrowing, heart-rhythm problems or reduced pumping function can appear later. Some people need another catheter procedure, valve intervention, surgery or medicines. Regular paediatric cardiology care should lead into specialist adult congenital-heart care, even when the person feels well.

Follow-up tests, including echocardiography and sometimes rhythm monitoring, exercise testing or cardiac MRI, depend on findings. Discuss new fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance or palpitations promptly; fainting, severe breathing difficulty or a new blue spell requires emergency care. Exercise advice is individual: many can enjoy ordinary activity, while significant remaining problems may require restrictions. Ask for a specific plan instead of a lifelong blanket ban on sport.

Daily care, dental health and family questions

Keep appointments, the treatment history and an accessible emergency plan. Ask for help with feeding, growth, development, school and emotional wellbeing when needed. Before non-heart surgery, invasive procedures or pregnancy planning later in life, discuss the heart condition with the congenital-heart team. A good outlook does not mean every person has identical needs or no future risk.

Good dental care matters because some people are at increased risk of infective endocarditis, an infection of the heart lining or valves. Antibiotics before certain dental procedures are for selected high-risk situations, such as unrepaired cyanotic disease, particular prosthetic valves/materials or residual defects; they are not automatic for every person or every procedure. Ask the cardiologist and dentist for the individual recommendation, and do not self-prescribe antibiotics.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the cardiac team to explain the exact anatomy, oxygen levels, proposed treatment and the plan for delivery or follow-up. A passed screening test does not replace assessment of new symptoms.

Keep a written emergency plan and ask the team to demonstrate any child-specific spell measures. Call emergency services for serious colour, breathing or responsiveness changes; do not delay for a home manoeuvre.

Agree long-term cardiac reviews, an activity plan and the individual dental-antibiotic advice. Request feeding, developmental and emotional support, and plan transition to adult congenital-heart services.

How BeMama can help

The four-part name does not describe the whole future of a child. An individual anatomy-based treatment plan, emergency guidance and continuing follow-up are more useful than assuming every blue baby has TOF or every repaired heart needs no further care.

When to seek help

Any of these signs requires emergency help now: sudden blue or grey lips, tongue or face, breathing difficulty, seizures, fainting or loss of consciousness, marked floppiness or severe difficulty waking. Follow a diagnosed child’s specialist spell plan while help is arranged; do not treat an undiagnosed blue baby with a generic position and wait. Report new or increasing spells even after improvement. Do not self-prescribe heart medicines or antibiotics, and do not stop follow-up because surgery has been completed.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • TOF combines four structural heart changes; its severity varies.
  • Neither the absence of blue colour nor a passed newborn screen fully rules out TOF.
  • Sudden blue or grey colour, breathing difficulty or reduced responsiveness needs emergency help.
  • Repair may be done in one operation or stages according to the baby’s needs.
  • Lifelong follow-up, tailored activity and individual dental advice remain important.

Frequently asked questions

What are the four changes in tetralogy of Fallot?

They are obstruction of the lung blood-flow pathway, a hole between the ventricles, an aorta overriding that hole and thickening of the right ventricular muscle. The degree and exact anatomy vary, including severe forms with pulmonary atresia.

Which symptoms may occur?

Rapid or difficult breathing, feeding fatigue, poor growth, irritability, prolonged crying, a murmur and blue or grey colour can occur. Low oxygen can cause fainting or seizures. Not every baby looks blue at birth, and symptoms alone do not establish the diagnosis.

Does a baby turning blue prove TOF?

No. Heart, lung, airway and other problems can cause low oxygen. Sudden blue or grey lips, tongue or face, breathing difficulty, floppiness, seizures or reduced responsiveness require emergency help now, without waiting to identify the cause.

Should I use the knees-to-chest position?

Only follow a specific spell plan taught by the cardiac team for a child with diagnosed TOF, while arranging emergency help. It is not a general substitute for assessment of an undiagnosed blue baby. A spell needs urgent attention even if the child seems to recover.

What causes it, and did a parent do something wrong?

Often no single cause is found. Genetic changes and several other factors can contribute, but a diagnosis does not show that a parent caused it. Genetics and pre-pregnancy counselling can clarify relevant risks; do not change prescription medicines without advice.

Can it be detected during pregnancy?

Yes, ultrasound may identify it and fetal echocardiography can assess the heart in detail. Some cases are missed, and no scan excludes every problem. A fetal-heart team can plan the place of birth and immediate newborn care when TOF is diagnosed.

Will one operation permanently cure it?

Repair improves blood flow, but some babies need staged treatment and some people need further procedures later. Valve leakage, narrowing or rhythm problems can develop. Lifelong congenital-heart follow-up remains important even with good health and no symptoms.

Are exercise limits and dental antibiotics needed for everyone?

No. Activity depends on heart function, residual problems and rhythm. Antibiotics before particular dental procedures are reserved for selected high-risk situations. Ask the cardiology team for your own recommendations instead of avoiding all exercise or taking antibiotics automatically.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
